steps.observation: You have 10 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three days when Elias heard the knock.

He paused midway up the spiral stairs, lamp oil in one hand, rag in the other. No boats had passed since the storm. No one came to Gullhook Light without a reason.

The knock sounded again, softer, as if whoever was outside was unsure they still existed.

Elias descended, joints creaking in rhythm with the old cast-iron steps. The door shuddered in its frame when he unlatched it; salt had swollen the wood, just as it had browned his beard and roughened his hands. He pulled it open a crack.

A girl stood on the threshold, dripping and shivering, hair plastered to her forehead. Behind her, the sea clawed at the rocks with white fingers.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” Elias said, because he couldn’t think of anything kinder.

“I saw your light,” she answered, as if that explained how anyone could have survived the wreck he’d watched break apart two nights before.

He had watched it: the black hull striking the hidden reef, the flare blooming uselessly in the storm, then darkness. He had rung the bell. He had called the coast guard until the radio crackled and died. In the end, he had done what he always did—kept the lens turning, kept the beam sweeping, because the sea did not stop to mourn.

“Come in,” he muttered, stepping aside.

She smelled of brine and diesel. Her jacket was torn, the ship’s emblem half-ripped from the sleeve. He recognized it: the freighter Morning Star. Fifty-two souls on board, the manifest had said. Fifty-two names on the list they’d read over the static two mornings ago. Fifty-two lost.

“Everyone else…” Elias began.

“I know,” she said, sitting when he pointed at the rickety chair by the stove. “I heard them.” Her voice sharpened. “They kept calling to you.”

He turned back to the counter to hide his face, busying himself with the kettle. “The radio was down.”

“Not on the radio.” She watched him closely, eyes dark as tide pools. “Out there.”

He stilled. The kettle hissed.

“Voices in the wind,” she went on. “In the water. ‘Tell him to keep the light on,’ they said. ‘Tell Elias we saw it.’”

He gripped the edge of the counter. No one knew why he’d taken this post. No one on the mainland cared who he had failed, years ago, before Gullhook, before he exiled himself to the edge of the world to atone by tending a lamp.

“You’re delirious,” he said.

She shook her head. “You think you’re alone up here. You think no one sees you. But they do. Every night, when you climb those stairs and wind the clockwork and wipe the salt from the glass, they’re watching. Grateful.”

The kettle screamed. He took it off the flame with shaking hands.

“How did you live?” he asked.

Her gaze drifted to the window, to the ragged line of foam where the reef lurked unseen. “A crate floated. Your light kept me from swimming the wrong way. I followed it until the rocks. I heard the voices again, telling me where to grab, when to duck. ‘He’s still there,’ they said. ‘He’s still trying.’” She looked back at him. “You don’t have to hear them for it to matter.”

He poured her tea. His eyes burned, but he blamed the steam.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

“Marin,” she said.

“Marin,” he repeated, as if testing whether it would vanish like a mirage. It stayed. She stayed.

For the first time in years, the lighthouse did not feel like a punishment.

When the coast guard boat finally appeared that afternoon, churning a white path through the grey, Elias stood outside with Marin. The wind snapped at their coats. The beam swept overhead, bright even in daylight—a great pale hand reaching out and back, out and back.

“You’ll go with them,” Elias said.

“Yes,” she replied. “But I’ll tell them about the light.”

He almost told her to tell them nothing. Let Gullhook remain a forgotten outpost, its keeper a nameless shadow. Then he looked at the girl who had followed a single blade of brightness through black water because some stubborn old man believed his task still meant something.

“Tell them,” he said instead.

After they left, the island grew quiet again. Evening fell, drawing a heavy curtain between sea and sky. Elias climbed the iron steps, his lantern swinging, his breath steady. At the top, the great lens waited, glass facets catching the last scraps of sun.

He checked the mechanism, wound the weights, trimmed the wick. The simple rituals of his chosen life.

He paused before lighting the lamp, listening.

Only the wind, only the sea—yet something inside those sounds had changed, or he had. He no longer heard accusation in the waves’ endless breaking. Only insistence.

Do your work, the water said. We go on.

Elias struck the match. Flame bloomed, small and sure. He touched it to the wick, and the lamp caught, swelling into a clear, unwavering glow.

Outside, the beam turned, sweeping the horizon, a promise cast into the dark: someone is awake. Someone is watching.

Far offshore, a trawler altered its course by a few invisible degrees, its captain glancing once toward the steady light on the cliff and nodding without thinking, as men had done for a hundred years.

In the tower, the keeper stood by his lamp, hand resting on the warm brass, and stayed at his post.
